raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to solve an intuitively attractive problem in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI): conventional drug-eluting stents (DES) provide effective acute lumen gain and antiproliferative drug delivery but leave a permanent metallic cage that may impair vasomotion, complicate future bypass or PCI, jail side branches, and contribute to very late restenosis or thrombosis. Early first-in-human ABSORB studies supported the biological concept. The first poly-L-lactic acid everolimus-eluting scaffold showed procedural feasibility in simple de novo lesions, modest neointimal growth, eventual recovery of vasomotion, and no early signal of thrombosis in very small cohorts [1], [2], [3], [4]. The second-generation Absorb BVS improved radial stability and imaging outcomes, encouraging randomized comparison with contemporary everolimus-eluting metallic stents [5].

The pivotal clinical evidence, however, revealed a central lesson: the scaffold concept was sound, but first-generation implementation was unforgiving. In ABSORB II, 1-year clinical outcomes appeared broadly comparable, but angiographic and vasomotor advantages were not convincingly demonstrated [6]. At 3 years, Absorb failed its co-primary endpoints and showed higher target-vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis than metallic everolimus-eluting stents [7]. ABSORB III met noninferiority for 1-year target-lesion failure in selected, relatively noncomplex lesions [8], while ABSORB China and ABSORB Japan similarly showed acceptable short-term efficacy in controlled settings [9], [10]. Yet broader and longer follow-up changed the interpretation. The AIDA all-comers trial was reported early for safety concerns and demonstrated substantially more device thrombosis with BVS despite similar target-vessel failure [11]. ABSORB IV, designed with better lesion selection and blinding, improved some early procedural and angina assessments but did not erase the safety concerns [12]. ABSORB III 3-year follow-up confirmed excess scaffold thrombosis and target-vessel myocardial infarction, especially in small vessels [13]. Five-year ABSORB III data suggested that the excess hazard diminished after approximately 3 years, consistent with completion of resorption, but cumulative outcomes remained worse than metallic DES [14].

Mechanistic work identified several interacting causes. Absorb had thick struts, limited overexpansion tolerance, reduced radiopacity, and greater sensitivity to undersizing, underexpansion, malapposition, and discontinuity during degradation. In pooled ABSORB analyses, careful vessel sizing, lesion preparation, and high-pressure post-dilatation were associated with improved outcomes [15]. Multicentre thrombosis analyses linked scaffold thrombosis to small lumen dimensions, suboptimal expansion, ostial lesions, reduced left ventricular function, and antiplatelet interruption [16]. Optical coherence tomography reports of very late thrombosis showed intraluminal scaffold dismantling, a failure mode distinct from metallic DES [17]. Quantitative coronary angiography confirmed that treating very small vessels carried disproportionate risk [18]. These findings crystallized the “PSP” approach—prepare, size appropriately, post-dilate—alongside avoidance of small, calcified, long, bifurcation, thrombotic, and overlapping scaffold segments.

Meta-analyses reinforced this temporal risk profile. Patient-level pooled analysis at 1 year showed broadly similar composite outcomes but numerically higher thrombosis [19]. By 2 years, the excess risk of device-oriented events and definite/probable thrombosis was clear [20]. Randomized-trial meta-analysis likewise showed more scaffold thrombosis with first-generation BVS than metallic everolimus-eluting stents [21]. Time-varying pooled data suggested that hazards concentrated during the active bioresorption phase and attenuated beyond 3 years [22]. Importantly, extended dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) has not fully solved the problem. An ABSORB pooled analysis suggested DAPT within the first year was strongly associated with lower myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis, whereas benefit beyond 1 year was not clearly demonstrated [23].

Consequently, first-generation polymeric Absorb BVS largely disappeared from routine practice. Nevertheless, the field has not disappeared. Magnesium-based resorbable scaffolds offer faster degradation, different mechanical behaviour, and potentially less late dismantling. BIOSOLVE-II showed promising 6-month safety and angiographic performance for the sirolimus-eluting absorbable magnesium scaffold [24]. Contemporary reviews emphasize that future success requires thinner struts, improved expansion latitude, better radiopacity, predictable resorption, optimized implantation, and randomized evidence against current ultrathin DES [25], [26], [27]. Registry data in diabetes and post-market studies remain hypothesis-generating rather than practice-changing [28], [29]. Newer thin-strut polymeric platforms, including Firesorb, have reported encouraging early outcomes, but durable comparative data are still needed before BVS can re-enter mainstream PCI [30].

Thus, bioresorbable scaffolds represent both a cautionary and instructive chapter in interventional cardiology. The long-term goal—temporary scaffolding followed by vascular restoration—remains compelling. The clinical reality is that early safety must match best-in-class DES before any late benefit can matter. Current use should be restricted to trials or carefully selected registries, with meticulous imaging-guided implantation and prolonged follow-up through and beyond complete resorption.
